summary: Food products for human consumption sold unprepared for home consumption are exempt from sales and use tax.

citations.title: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 6359(a)
citations.quote: There are exempted from the taxes imposed by this part the gross receipts from the sale of, and the storage, use, or other consumption in this state of, food products for human consumption.

citations.title: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 6359(b)(1)
citations.quote: Cereals and cereal products, oleomargarine, meat and meat products, fish and fish products, eggs and egg products, vegetables and vegetable products, fruit and fruit products

notes: 1992-12-01 is when Proposition 163 took effect and set subdivision (b)'s current list (section history). Staples were exempt before that too, but the exemption's original enactment date was not verified from the fetched sources. Between 1991-07-15 and 1992-11-30 'snack foods' and candy were taxable; the code excludes candy, so that period isn't modeled separately. notes: The code says 'sold with eating utensils the seller provides', but California has no utensil test: courts have held a paper napkin isn't 'tableware' (Treasure Island Catering, annotated under 6359), though sandwiches on non-returnable cardboard trays counted (Hart's Drive-In). summary: Food sold uncooked for the buyer to cook (a take-and-bake pizza, raw kebabs, a meal kit) is exempt in California as food products for home consumption: food that requires further processing is not in a form suitable for consumption on the seller's premises, so the 80-80 rule for cold food to go does not reach it.

citations.title: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 6359(a)
citations.quote: There are exempted from the taxes imposed by this part the gross receipts from the sale of, and the storage, use, or other consumption in this state of, food products for human consumption.

citations.quote: Food products that require further processing are not in a form "suitable for immediate consumption."

citations.quote: Food products that require further processing are also considered not in a form suitable for immediate consumption.

citations.title: State Board of Equalization letter of March 27, 1985 (Annotation 550.0104)
citations.quote: In addition, sales of food products when furnished in a form not suitable for consumption on the seller’s premises remain exempt.

citations.title: 18 CCR 1603(c)(2)
citations.quote: The term does not include cold food products which obviously would not be consumed on the premises of the seller, e.g., a cold party tray or a whole cold chicken.

notes: No California source read names take-and-bake pizza, raw kebabs or meal kits; the rule rests on Annotation 550.0104's reading that food requiring further processing (its examples: syrup to be mixed, frozen food to be defrosted) is not in a form suitable for immediate consumption, so the 80-80 rule (Rev. & Tax. Code 6359(d)(6), Regulation 1603(c)) does not tax it, and on Regulation 1603(c)(2)'s exclusion of cold food that obviously would not be consumed on the premises. Uncooked food is not hot prepared food. Starts at 1992-12-01 like CA's food.grocery rule. Food served for eating at the seller's tables, or sold within a place charging admission, is taxed under other parts of 6359(d); not expected for uncooked food and not modeled. The state, Bradley-Burns local and district taxes share the base. 2026-11-02: cited page moved from https://www.cdtfa.ca.gov/lawguides/vol1/sutl/6359.html to https://cdtfa.ca.gov/lawguides/vol1/sutl/6359.html. 2026-11-02: cited page moved from https://www.cdtfa.ca.gov/lawguides/vol2/suta/550-0104.html to https://cdtfa.ca.gov/lawguides/vol2/suta/550-0104.html. 2026-11-02: cited page moved from https://www.cdtfa.ca.gov/lawguides/annotations/550-0104.pdf to https://cdtfa.ca.gov/lawguides/annotations/550-0104.pdf. 2026-11-02: cited page moved from https://www.cdtfa.ca.gov/lawguides/vol1/sutr/1603.html to https://cdtfa.ca.gov/lawguides/vol1/sutr/1603.html.

summary: Clothing, footwear, accessories and protective or sport gear sold at retail are taxable at California general state, local and district sales-tax rates.

citations.title: California Tax Service Center — What Is Taxable?
citations.quote: Examples include furniture, giftware, toys, antiques and clothing.

citations.title: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code 6051, CDTFA Law Guide
citations.quote: For the privilege of selling tangible personal property at retail a tax is hereby imposed upon all retailers

notes: The taxable-items page is verified in its October 17, 2026 Internet Archive capture. Section 6051 dates the general retail levy to August 1, 1933, but this draft does not project clothing-specific evidence back to that date. No ordinary clothing price threshold or subtype exemption found. Local and district sales taxes use the general tangible-property base as in the existing California rules.

summary: Alcoholic beverages sold in containers or served on premises are taxable at the general California sales-tax rates. Separate alcoholic-beverage excise taxes are outside this rule.

citations.title: CDTFA Publication 22, Dining and Beverage Industry (January 2025), Beverages
citations.quote: Sales of the following beverages are always taxable: • Carbonated beverages such as soda or sparkling water • Alcoholic beverages

citations.title: CDTFA Regulation 1602(a)(2), Food Products
citations.quote: "Food products" does not include carbonated or effervescent bottled waters, spirituous, malt or vinous liquors, or carbonated beverages.

citations.title: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code 6051, CDTFA Law Guide
citations.quote: For the privilege of selling tangible personal property at retail a tax is hereby imposed upon all retailers

notes: Publication 22 is dated January 2025; January 1 represents the publication month rather than a tax change. Regulation 1602 excludes spirituous, malt and vinous liquors from the food exemption. State, Bradley-Burns local and district taxes share the ordinary tangible-property base as in the existing California rules.
